opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are pretty reasonable.

One is that the whole thing just sounds too simple. If you've spent years in machine learning, you're used to progress coming from clever ideas: a new architecture, a better training trick, some insight into the structure of the problem. So when someone says, "Actually, you mostly just make the model bigger, give it more data, train it longer, and it gets better in a predictable way," that feels almost insulting to the craft. It's natural to assume there must be a catch.

A second reason is that people have seen plenty of trends break before. Experienced researchers have watched curves flatten and techniques that worked on toy problems fall apart at scale. So when they see a smooth line on a log plot, their instinct is to ask where it bends. That's healthy scepticism. The trouble is that with scaling laws, people kept predicting the bend, and for a long time it just didn't come. Loss kept going down across many orders of magnitude of compute.

Third, there's a gap between "the loss goes down" and "the model gets smarter." Next-token prediction loss is an abstract number. Someone can reasonably say: fine, the model is better at predicting text, but why should that mean it can reason, write code, or do science? That link wasn't obvious in advance. Part of what changed people's minds was seeing it in practice: as loss improved, models picked up capabilities nobody explicitly trained for. Still, if you hadn't watched that happen up close, it's a big leap.

Then there are concrete objections that deserve to be taken seriously. Will we run out of high-quality data? Can we keep getting compute, given the cost and the physical constraints of building ever larger clusters? Are there capabilities, like long-horizon planning or real-world agency, that won't fall out of predicting text? These aren't silly questions. I don't think anyone can say with certainty that scaling continues forever.

My own view, from working on this directly, is that the burden of proof has shifted. The trend has held for a long time and across a lot of scale, and each time someone named a specific wall, we either didn't hit it or found a way around it, whether through synthetic data, better data filtering, or new training methods layered on top. So I'd take the specific objections seriously, but I'd be wary of the general intuition that "it can't be this simple." So far, to a surprising degree, it has been.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling can feel too simple to researchers accustomed to clever new ideas, but it does not connect that skepticism to intuitions about how humans learn.

r002.rationale: The response raises possible data and compute constraints, but does not say implementation mistakes can make additional compute fail to improve performance.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss difficulty distinguishing implementation mistakes from fundamental scaling limits when more compute fails to help.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few things going on. The first is just that if you look at the history of the field, scaling has not been the obvious bet for most of it. For a long time the way you made progress in machine learning was by having a clever idea: a better architecture, a better training objective, some inductive bias that captured something about the structure of the problem. And a lot of the people who are most technically knowledgeable came up in that world. So there's a natural intuition that the interesting work is the ideas, and that just making the same thing bigger is kind of a dumb strategy that shouldn't work. It's almost offensive to that way of thinking that you could get so far by just adding more compute and more data.

The second thing is that the scaling laws are really unintuitive if you haven't stared at them. When we train models, what we actually see is that the loss goes down in this very smooth, predictable way as you add compute. That's a surprising empirical fact. But the thing people care about isn't the loss, it's capabilities. And capabilities often look discontinuous. A model goes from not being able to do arithmetic to being able to do arithmetic, or from not being able to write code to being able to write code. So if you're looking at it from the outside, it can feel like each new capability is a separate thing you need to explain, rather than the downstream consequence of a very smooth underlying trend. And it's easy to look at any given model and say, "well, it can't do X, and I don't see how making it bigger would ever let it do X."

The third thing, and I think this is actually the strongest version of the sceptical argument, is that lower loss isn't obviously the same as being smarter. You could imagine a world where the model gets better and better at predicting the next token, but all that improvement is going into memorising more trivia or getting slightly better at modelling the quirks of internet text, rather than into anything that looks like reasoning. That's a legitimate hypothesis. I just think it's turned out to be wrong so far. Every time we've scaled, the models have gotten better at the things we actually care about, not just at the narrow objective. But I can see why someone would have predicted otherwise, and it's not a crazy prior.

And then honestly, I think there's a bit of motivated reasoning in both directions. People who work at labs that are scaling have an incentive to believe it'll keep working. People who are sceptical often have a view of intelligence where it just seems like it should require something more than pattern matching on a lot of data. I'd say I was somewhat sceptical myself before I saw it up close. What changed my mind wasn't an argument, it was watching the trend hold up over and over again when there were lots of reasons to think it might stop.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling conflicts with intuitions favoring clever ideas over simply making models bigger, but it does not connect that skepticism to intuitions about how humans learn.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention implementation mistakes in scaling experiments or their effect on performance.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss difficulty distinguishing implementation mistakes from fundamental scaling limits.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that scaling sounds like a very naive approach. If you’re used to solving technical problems, you expect progress to come from understanding what’s missing and designing something that fixes it. The idea that you can take roughly the same system, make it bigger, train it on more data, and get qualitatively new capabilities is pretty surprising.

And people have reasonable intuitions about diminishing returns. They look at a model making an elementary mistake and think, “Surely you need a different approach to fix that.” Sometimes that’s right. But it’s been difficult to predict which limitations will persist and which will go away with scale.

I’d distinguish being sceptical that scaling will continue forever — which seems entirely reasonable — from being confident that it’s about to stop working. The latter needs more evidence than pointing to something current models can’t do. At the same time, the fact that scaling has worked so far doesn’t establish that it will get us all the way. That’s still an empirical question.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling conflicts with expectations about solving technical problems, but does not connect that skepticism to intuitions about how humans learn.

r002.rationale: It does not state that implementation mistakes in scaling experiments can prevent additional compute from improving performance.

r003.rationale: It discusses uncertainty about which limitations will persist, but does not identify the difficulty of distinguishing implementation mistakes from fundamental scaling limits.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that, if you understand how these systems are trained, the thing we’re asking them to do sounds quite limited. You’re predicting the next token in a piece of text. And it’s very natural to think, “Well, you can get really good at that by picking up statistical patterns, but surely that’s different from actually understanding the world.”

The reason I’m less persuaded by that argument is that predicting text well can require understanding the processes that produced it. If you’re predicting what someone will say about an experiment, it helps to understand the experiment. If you’re predicting the next line of a mathematical proof, it helps to be able to do mathematics. So the training objective can sound simple while the capabilities that help you achieve it are quite general.

There’s still a separate question about how far scaling takes you. We have evidence that more compute and data improve these systems, but that doesn’t establish that every capability will keep improving indefinitely, or that scaling alone will get us everything we want. I think the sceptical intuition is understandable. I just wouldn’t treat the simplicity of the training objective as a strong reason to expect a ceiling.

r001.rationale: The response links skepticism to the apparently limited next-token objective and doubts about understanding, but does not mention intuitions about how humans learn.

r002.rationale: It does not say implementation mistakes in scaling experiments can prevent additional compute from improving performance.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss difficulty distinguishing implementation mistakes from fundamental scaling limits.
